## SIO bus communication

The 8051’s serial port is used for communication across the SIO bus, so the firmware doesn’t have to bit-bang
the serial bus data. It is driven in mode 0, giving a baud rate of 7.37MHz ÷ 12 ÷ 32 = 19.192KHz. The firmware
does not use RI/TI interrupts and uses polling for both receive and transmit.
The SIO command signal is connected to the timer 0 (T0) input, which is driven low when SIO command is
asserted. It too is polled by the firmware.
SIO ready is connected to the INT1 input and does use an interrupt. The firmware powers down the motors and
idles the print mechanism while waiting for the computer to turn on.
## Horizontal positioning

The print head is horizontally positioned by the space motor under MCU control, sequentially activating motor
phases to move the print head back and forth. However, the space motor is not a stepper motor, and print
columns aren’t aligned to the phases. Instead, the firmware uses software delays to time the print columns
accurately between the phases, and also varies the speed.
Every four steps turns the motor shaft 30° and moves the print head by 2.54 mm or 1/10th of an inch.55 The
phases are numbered such that activating ascending phases (1, 2, …) moves the print head left and activating
descending numbered phases move the print head right.
In 5 CPI and 10 CPI modes, the firmware activates pairs of adjacent phases at a time, stepping phases every
~4060 machine cycles. One machine cycle on the 8051 takes 12 T-states, so this is about 38 characters/second.
Columns are printed 1350 cycles apart in 10 CPI mode for 12 columns per character. This timing is doubled to
2700 cycles per column in 5 CPI mode. The head is returned to home position slightly more slowly at 4120
cycles per phase step, also activating pairs of phases at a time.
In 16.5 CPI mode, the firmware alternates stepping with single and paired phases, i.e. 4, 4+3, 3, 3+2, 2, 2+1, 1,
1+4. The motor has more torque when two phases are activated, so the firmware compensates by varying the
time delay between steps, using ~2040 cycles with two phases and ~4700 cycles with single phase. Columns
are still printed 1350 cycles apart, so the character rate is the same but the head movement rate slows
proportionally to the higher density.

## 9.8 1029 Programmable Printer

The 1029 is a dot-matrix printer capable of printing 80 columns on regular 8.5” paper. In addition to regular text
output, it also has bitmap graphics capability.
SIO device ID
The 1029 responds to SIO device IDs $40 (P: or P1:) and $45 (P6:). All other printer device IDs are ignored.
Write command
Write ($57) is used to send character data to the printer. The data frame size is 40 bytes and may include a
complete or partial line. If an EOL ($9B) is present in the buffer, the line is ended at the first EOL and bytes after
the EOL are ignored. Otherwise, the printer processes the characters in the data frame, buffering characters in
an internal line buffer and printing a line if it is full. Thus, multiple Write commands are needed to build up an 80
character line.
The 820 mode byte in AUX1 is ignored by the 1029. It will accept Write commands with any mode byte, but if it
receives the sideways ($53) mode, it still expects a 40 byte data frame. This leads to 138 (timeout) errors from
CIO if sideways mode is enabled on the P: handler since in that case the handler tries to send a 29 byte data
frame.
When a line is full or ended with EOL, the printer prints the line before sending the Complete ($45) code to the
computer, after the line is printed but without waiting for the head to finish returning to the left.
The 1029 lacks a paper sensor, and will not return Error ($45) for an out of paper condition or any other
condition. The only way a Write command fails is via a NAK ($4E) if a data frame checksum error is detected.
Line overflow
As with the 1025, the 1029 prints a line as soon as its line buffer is full. It also avoids printing a blank line if an
EOL is received after an exactly full line is printed.
Status command
The status command ($53) returns a canned status response of $00, $00, $14, $29 which never changes. The
printer does not even support the invalid command/data frame bits in the first byte.
The 1029 clears its line buffer and resets to default state when the status command is processed. This includes
disabling underlining, international characters, elongation, bit image mode, and reverting to 6 LPI spacing.
Escape processing
Special modes are selected in the 1029 through escape codes, which consist of the ESC character ($1B)
followed by a character selecting the escape code. Unlike the 1025, all escape codes can be issued anywhere in
a line, and more mid-line mode changes are supported. However, the 1029 does not allow bit 7 to be set on the
escape code and will not recognize escape sequences using them.
Repeated ESC characters are treated the same as a single ESC character, so ESC ESC A is treated the same
as ESC A. Unrecognized escape sequences are ignored and eat the unrecognized escape code character. ESC
EOL is ignored but still treated as end of line.
Escape sequences do not have to be contained within a single Write command and can be split across
commands.

Dot matrix
Characters are printed within a 5x7 dot matrix. The baseline is at the bottom and there is no descender space,
so characters like g and q are raised. There is no half-column spacing as in the 1025. A blank column separates
characters in the same line.
As the printer is specified to print 80 characters across at 10 characters per inch and back to back lines at 9 lines
per inch, dots are spaced approximately 0.0167” apart horizontally and 0.0159” vertically.
International character mode
The normal 1029 character set consists of the ASCII characters $20-7F, with $7F (DEL) producing a solid block.
ATASCII characters that differ in this range are not supported; Home ($7B), for instance, prints {. Bit 7 is ignored
for characters besides ESC/EOL and the control characters $00-1A / $1C-1F are ignored without printing
anything.
ESC CTRL+W switches to international character mode, enabling characters $00-1A, $1C-1F and replacing $60,
$7B, and $7D-7F with the corresponding characters from the international ATASCII character set. ESC CTRL+X
switches back to normal character mode. International character mode can be toggled on and off mid-line and
both international and normal characters mixed within the same line.
Figure 21: 1029 character set
Line spacing
By default, lines are printed with a spacing of 6 lines per inch (LPI), which results in about a 3.5 dot row high gap
in between lines. ESC 9 switches from 6 LPI to 9 LPI spacing, which places lines vertically adjacent to each
other. ESC 6 changes back to 6 LPI spacing.
Unlike the 1025, line spacing can be changed during the middle of a line. The line spacing mode that is active
when the line is ended or filled is the one that takes effect. If exactly 80 characters are printed at 6 LPI followed
by ESC 9, the 80 characters are printed, a 6 LPI advance occurs, and then the spacing is switched to 9 LPI for
the next line.
Elongated mode
ESC CTRL+N switches from normal 10 CPI characters to 5 CPI elongated characters. In this mode, the column
patterns for each character are doubled up horizontally and each character takes two character columns. ESC
CTRL+O switches back to normal width characters. Unlike the 1025, the 1029 can switch to elongated
characters in the middle of a line. Elongation persists across lines until turned off.
Chapter 9 -  Serial I/O (SIO) Bus
243

--- Page 244 ---

Altirra Hardware Reference Manual
Created by Avery Lee
Although elongated characters take two character positions, they can be started at both even and odd positions.
If an elongated character is printed at column 79 where there is not enough space for one, the line is ended and
the elongated character is pushed to the next line.
Underlining
ESC CTRL+Y enables underlining for characters. The underline is printed as an additional row of solid dots two
rows beneath the main line, with one line of blank dots in between and roughly between rows at 6 LPI. The
printer does this by doing a 9 LPI advance, printing the underlines at the 2nd row of the next line, then advancing
the paper by the remaining distance. Underlining persists until turned off again with ESC CTRL+Z or EOL is
reached; underlining will stay enabled when printing lines longer than 80 characters.
For each character underlined, the 5 dots underneath the 5x7 cell and the 6th dot to the right are printed. The
underline is therefore continuous for adjacent characters. All characters are underlined including spaces, but the
underline stops at an EOL.
Underlining is intended to be used with 6 LPI spacing. If it is enabled with 9 LPI spacing, the underline overlaps
with the next line printed.
Bit image mode
ESC CTRL+A enters bit image mode for graphics output. In this mode, the control bytes from the computer
directly drive the seven dot columns of the printer, allowing full control over the printer’s output.
The ESC CTRL+A sequence is directly followed by two bytes giving the length of the bitmap data in bytes as a
16-bit binary number, MSB first. Graphics data then follows as a byte per column, with bit 0 controlling the
bottom dot and bit 6 controlling the top dot; bit 7 is ignored and ESC/EOL processing is suspended. The printer
switches back out of bit image mode and resumes interpreting bytes as characters once the specified number of
bit image bytes is processed. A full line requires 480 bytes of bitmap data.
For contiguous graphics taller than one line, 9 LPI mode must be selected to place lines vertically adjacent to
each other. This is not automatic for bit image graphics and by default the printer will use the normal 6 LPI line
spacing, which produces a gap in between.
Bit image mode may be started and stopped mid-line, mixing text and graphics. This can result in text characters
being printed out of their normal alignment, allowing fine horizontal positioning without needing to render the text
itself as graphics.
If the length value specified in the ESC CTRL+A sequence exceeds the remaining number of columns in the line,
it is effectively clamped as the printer ends bit image mode anyway at the end of the line, and then interprets the
remaining data as text. A length value of 0 is valid and is effectively a no-op.
Underlining is suspended during bit image graphics. If bit image graphics are started when underlining is
enabled, the state is preserved and the underlining resumed for text printed after exiting bit image mode, but the
bit image graphics themselves will not have an underline.
Line wrapping
The printer rasterizes text or graphics into an internal buffer until either 480 columns are filled or an EOL is
processed, then prints the line and resets the line buffer. For text, this is equivalent to a limit of 80 characters
(normal) or 40 characters (elongated). However, the limit is more complex when graphics are involved.
Bit image graphics will fill as many columns as are provided or remain in the line, whichever is shorter. A
maximum of 480 columns can fit within a line. If the line is filled before the image length is reached, bit image
mode is forcibly disabled early and the remaining characters are processed as text instead of graphics.

Altirra Hardware Reference Manual
Created by Avery Lee
A text character takes 5 columns followed by 1 column of spacing in normal mode, or 10 + 2 columns in
elongated mode. If the character does not completely fit, the line is printed and the character put at the start of
the next line. If the character fits within the line but the spacing doesn’t, the character is still put within the line
and the extra spacing extends into the right margin. This means that one column of bit image graphics can be
printed followed by 80 characters within one line. However, printing 80 characters + 1 column bit image results in
line being flushed after 80 characters, followed by the bit image being put at the beginning of the next line.
There is an anomaly if underlining is enabled and the spacing after a character overlaps the right margin. In this
case, the underlining will be drawn under the following spacing as usual, even if it extends beyond the 480th
column. For instance, printing 1 column of bit image graphics followed by 80 underlined characters will result in
the underline being drawn into the 481st column. Elongated characters can extend the underline to the 482nd
column.
Polish character set

characters are in the $00-1A range:

An additional 1024 x 4-bit static RAM provides bit image data storage, since 480 columns of 7-bit dot patterns
must be stored to print a line. The static RAM’s data lines are connected to AD0-AD3 on the 8039.
## Head positioning mechanism

The head solenoid and motor enables control the left and right movement of the head across the platen. The
motor, when enabled, pulls the head toward the right at a constant speed of approximately 5 inches per second.
Activating the head solenoid disconnects the motor from the carriage and allows a spring to retract the head
back to the far left, at a somewhat faster rate than it normally advances. The home sensor signal received on
P2.7 indicates when the print head has reached the home position at the far left. While disengaged, the motor
can still be activated; this is used by the firmware to bring the motor up to speed before engaging it for better
speed consistency.
## Dot printing mechanism

The 1029’s print head design is unusual in having only a single hammer to print all of the dots in the dot matrix.

This design is shared by some other printers including the CBM MPS-801 and Amstrad DMP1, which share a
similar Seikosha design. However, the 1029 differs in some implementation details such as the dot timing pattern
and the polarity of some signals.
When the motor is enabled, the platen rotates at a high speed at the same time. Bumps on the platen sweep
down the print area, raising different points on the paper. This allows the print hammer to impact only one point
on the page at a time. The platen bump sweeps down through the print area once for each column so that each
of the seven dots of the column can be printed before moving to the next column.
A dot timing signal is provided to the 8039 on the T1 input to accurately time the activation of the print hammer.
The dot signal is normally low and receives a series of 7 high pulses when each dot in the column should be
printed. There is an idle period of approximately two dot times (or ~0.9ms from pulse start to pulse start)
between each column to give the head time to advance and to indicate to the MCU when each column starts.
The firmware relies on the dot timing signal pattern being received whenever the motor is running, even if it is
disengaged from the carriage by the head solenoid.
During the printing of each column, the head is continuously moving right, which would normally cause a slight
rightward skew of the printed output due to the successive delays in printing each dot. The print head is angled
slightly oppositely to counteract this so that the printed dots in each column are vertically aligned.
Line feed motor
Port 1 bits P1.2, P1.3, and P1.4 control the 4-phase line feed motor that advances the paper. P1.4 is the power
enable and is pulled low to activate a motor phase; P1.2 and P1.3 select the phase to activate. The sequence to
advance the paper is 00, 01, 11, 10, with P1.2 turning on first. The paper advances by 1/144th of an inch with
each successive phase, so phases are advanced 16 times for 9 LPI spacing and 24 times for 6 LPI spacing.
## 9.10 850 Interface Module

The 850 Interface Module connects four serial ports and a parallel port to the computer.
Firmware versions
There are at least two known versions of the 850 firmware, which is 4K in size. An early revision has a CRC32 of
[9201359A], while the common later revision has CRC32 [2CF990B9].
Known differences between the revisions:
The R: handler in the early revision disables concurrent mode I/O when the Break key is pressed. The
- 
newer version instead suppresses the Break key. Note that both behaviors happen even with OS-A,
which doesn’t have a dedicated Break key vector.
The early revision only responds to the device ID for P:/P1:. The later revision also responds to P2:.
- 
The timeout for printer operations was raised from $05 (320 vblanks) to $1F (1984 vblanks).

Note
There are multiple versions of the 850 documentation. The 1980 version of the Atari 850 Interface Module
Operator’s Manual documents the early firmware behavior of turning off concurrent I/O when Break is

manual notes the newer behavior of suppressing Break with a note about the older firmware.
Serial port functionality
Four 9-pin RS-232 compatible serial ports are exposed on the 850. They can either all be used together at low
speed up to 300 baud, or a single port can be used at high speed up to 9600 baud.
The serial ports are asymmetric in hardware capabilities. All four ports support bidirectional full duplex
communication and the DTR signal, but only ports 1-3 support DSR, only ports 1 and 4 support RTS, and only
port 1 supports CTS. Port 4 does not sensing or controlling any handshaking signals, with RTS and DTR
connected but hardwired high.
RS-232 SIO addressing
The RS-232 ports are addressed using the SIO addresses $50-53.

baud rate must be 300 baud or less, or the command will fail.
The returned data payload for the stream command consists of nine bytes to be written to $D200-D208 (AUDF1-
AUDCTL) to configure POKEY for the correct baud rate during the transfer. Afterward, the controller starts
operating in streaming mode.
Streaming mode causes the controller to reflect between the Atari SIO bus and the serial port. During streaming,
no commands can be sent to the controller, and in particular, it is not possible to read the control line status. The
controller exits streaming mode the next time that the command line is asserted.
At higher speeds, the maximum baud rate is limited by the resolution at which the controller firmware can mirror
signals between the port and the SIO bus. The firmware updates outputs about every 28μs on average, giving a
mediocre resolution of ~3.7 samples per bit at the top speed of 9600 baud.

Automatic handler load
The 850 contains an R: handler in ROM that is downloadable to the computer, allowing the 850 to be used
without having to load a handler from disk or include it in a cartridge. This handler can be loaded in three ways:
Fake disk boot, if no disk drive is attached and powered on as D1:.
- 
Loaded by the default AUTORUN.SYS that comes with DOS 2.0S, after DOS boots.
- 
Loaded by a program that knows how to use the 850-specific bootstrap commands.
- 
Upon bootstrap, the R: handler registers itself in HATABS and becomes available though the OS CIO facility,
including the BASIC OPEN command. The R: handler itself is relocatable and is loaded at the base of
application memory at MEMLO, raising MEMLO up to after the handler. Thus, the R: handler can either load
after DOS, or as low as $0700 if DOS is not loaded.
For early ROM revisions, the R: handler raises MEMLO by 1762 ($06E2) bytes, and for the common ROM
revision, 1728 ($06C0) bytes. For DOS 2.0S in default configuration, the higher MEMLO requires programs to
position themselves higher to around $2400 instead of the default $2000 as used by many programs.
Because the R: handler can relocate itself to any arbitrary byte address, its performance can vary slightly
depending on the low address byte where it is loaded. This happens because different load addresses can
change which branches and indexing operations in the handler code cross a page, causing them to take slightly
longer.
Type 1/2 Poll command
Command $3F polls the SIO bus for devices with automatically loadable handlers. The 850 responds to this
command in one of two ways. For the standard poll with AUX1=$00, it responds once to the very last (26th)
attempt. It always responds to AUX1=$01. The result of the command is a 12-byte DCB to use with the SIOV
vector to retrieve the booter/relocator, which is then invoked at $0506.58 This program then loads, relocates, and
initializes the handler at MEMLO, after which MEMLO is raised to above the handler.
Booter/relocator download command
Command $21 (!) loads the booter/relocator from the device directly with using a poll command. The
booter/relocator is returned in a single block, so the size must be known beforehand. This command is usually
not issued directly, but according to the DCB returned by the poll command. AUX1/2 are ignored.
Early ROM revisions return 345 ($0159) bytes from this command, while the common revision returns 342
($0156) bytes. This means that $0500-0658 must be available to bootstrap the 850.
Handler download command
Command $26 (&) is used to load the peripheral handler from the device; AUX1/2 are ignored. Unlike the similar
command used by Type 3/4 Polls, the 850 does not return the handler in blocks. Instead, it is returned as a
single large block. This means that the handler size must be known beforehand. This command is usually not
[58] As noted earlier, DOS II's AUTORUN.SYS hardcodes $0506 as the start address, so this can be relied upon.

Created by Avery Lee
issued directly, but automatically by the booter/relocator.
Early ROM revisions return 1460 ($05B4) bytes from this command. The common revision returns 1496 ($0592)
bytes.
Diskless bootstrap
To support using the 850 without DOS, such as with a telecommunications cartridge, the 850 supports a fake
disk boot (type 0 poll) to load the R: handler into memory. The 850 simulates a disk drive on D1: and returns
three boot sectors with a load address of $0500. The boot sectors contain the same relocator bootstrap code as
returned by command $21, except for some additional unused data being returned at the end of the third sector.
The extra data is from after where the relocator is stored in the 850 firmware ROM, containing the first part of the
handler download.
A couple of safeguards are in place to avoid interfering with a real disk drive. The fake disk boot process is
initiated by the Get Sector command sent by the OS boot process, but the 850 waits until 26 consecutive Get
Sector commands have been sent to D1: before responding to the 27th command with $08 00 01 00 09. This
also unlocks the Read Sector command for sectors 1-3. Those sectors can be read in any order, but any other
command to D1: -- including another Get Sector command or Read Sector for any sector other 1-3 –
permanently disables the fake boot process until the 850 is reset. The relocator/handler download commands,
however, are not disabled.
Reset behavior
Like most SIO devices, the 850 is not reset when the computer is reset, as it is unaware of when that occurs.
However, it does monitor the SIO Ready signal line and resets itself if the computer is turned off.
Printer support
The 850 also supports a parallel printer port, using the standard printer SIO protocol. The printer commands are
only responded to if a printer is connected and not in fault status.
The original firmware only supports device ID $40 (P:/P1:). The newer firmware also supports $41 (P2:).
Printer status command
A printer status command ($53) responds with a four-byte status frame as follows:

Byte 1
D7=1: Always set
D2=1: Printer timeout
D1=1: Bad data frame bit (framing or checksum error)
D0=1: Bad command frame bit (unsupported command or bad orientation)
Byte 2
AUX1 of last valid printer command (status or write)
Byte 3
Timeout low ($05 or $1E)
Byte 4
Timeout high ($00)
Table 37: 850 printer status frame

--- Page 253 ---

Altirra Hardware Reference Manual
Created by Avery Lee
($4E) with a 40 byte frame; any other orientation is NAKed.
The data frame is processed up to an including any EOL ($9B); characters after the first EOL are ignored. An
EOL, if present, is transformed to a CR ($0D) before being sent. Additionally, whenever two EOLs are sent in a
row, a space is written in between to ensure that the printer prints a blank line.
Printing is synchronous. There is no buffering and the write command will block until all characters are written or
a timeout occurs. The 850 itself implements a 5 or 30 second timeout for the entire write, depending on the
firmware revision. If a timeout occurs, the remainder of the write is discarded, the printer timeout error bit is set,
and Error is returned.
A successful printer write will clear all printer error status bits.
The 850 allows printer writes to be interrupted by another command. Asserting the SIO command line while a
printer write operation is in progress causes the 850 to terminate the write operation and prepare to receive a
new command frame.
## 9.11 835 Modem

The Atari 835 modem is an SIO bus peripheral that allows phone line based communications at 300 baud with
Bell 103 modem compatible modulation. It was shipped with the Telelink II communications software cartridge.
Command protocol
The 835 does not use the standard SIO protocol and communicates exclusively at 300 baud. Commands are
distinguished by the SIO command line being asserted while command bytes are sent, also at 300 baud. The
motor control line is not used, so the 835 is always active. In particular, this means that the 835’s command
bytes and standard SIO command frames are constantly being received by both the 835 and other devices, with
framing and checksum errors preventing the devices from misinterpreting the data.
Modem processing
Data transmission starts suspended and must be explicitly resumed before communications can take place.
When resumed, the 835 transfers data between the SIO bus and the modem.
The 835 continuously runs four shift registers in software: SIO input, SIO output, modem input, and modem
output. Shift processing occurs at 1200Hz with all four shifters running at 300 baud, so the 835 can sample with
quarter bit phase precision. The firmware receives and retransmits bytes between the SIO and modem ports, so
bits are “reconditioned” in the process and are retimed at 300 baud regardless of the original transmission rate.
This also allows for one byte of buffering in each shift register, though the 835 has no ability to catch up since all
shifters run at 300 baud and there is no provision for flow control.
The modem processing loop also monitors the SIO ready and carrier detect states. If SIO ready drops, indicating
that the computer is turned off, the 835 will automatically reset itself. Changes in carrier detect state are
monitored to handle the various dial / answer processes.
Code
Command
Description

Switches to the originating modem set band (1270Hz/1070Hz).
$4A (“J”)

Switches to the answering modem set band (2225Hz/2025Hz).
$4B (“K”)

Commands $4E-$50 (“N” through “P”) and $54-56 (“T” through “V”) are ignored and not handled by the firmware.
Some of them are commands only supported by the 1030 or XM301, or have different definitions in the T:
handler software.
If the modem is suspended and thus processing SIO commands, only the Reset Modem (“Q”) and Resume
Modem (“Y”) commands are handled. All other commands are ignored.
The SIO command line should be asserted before the start of the byte and deasserted after the end of the byte.
In particular, the two processing modes have different quirks in this regard. The modem processing loop simply
requires SIO command to be asserted when the stop bit is processed.
Command validation bug
Command bytes in the range of $80-FF are ignored by the firmware, but bytes within $00-7F and outside of the
range $48-5A (H-Z) can cause the 835 to malfunction. This is due to missing validation in the firmware, resulting
in it overrunning the bounds of a jump table and jumping to random locations within the code page that handles
commands. This only applies when normal command processing is enabled and not specialized command
processing, like the pulse dialing loop.
Signaling
The 1030 modem is one of the rare devices that uses the SIO proceed and interrupt control lines. The proceed
line is used to signal that communication can proceed, while the interrupt line indicates the carrier detect state.
These are intended to drive the PIA interrupt facility in order to assert IRQs on the 6502.
Both signals are momentarily pulled low for one tick at the modem processing rate of 1200Hz, lasting for 833μs.
The SIO proceed signal pulses when a command finishes, and the SIO interrupt signal pulses on a change in
the carrier detect state.
Command behavior
$48 (H) – Send break signal
Sends a long space (0 bit) signal to the remote side, often interpreted as a request to interrupt an operation. The
controller waits for any currently buffered bytes to finish shifting, then suspends the shifters and pulls the modem
transmit line low. After half a second, the transmit line is raised, the shifters are re-enabled, and regular
Chapter 9 -  Serial I/O (SIO) Bus
254

--- Page 255 ---

Altirra Hardware Reference Manual
Created by Avery Lee
communication resumes. SIO proceed is pulsed both after the command and when the break is finished.
As the SIO input shifter is also suspended during this process, no commands can be issued until the break
completes.
$49/$4A (I/J) – Set originate/answer mode
These commands select the tone set used by the modem, choosing the “polarity” of the communication. One
side must use the originating tone pair while the other side must use the answering tone pair, or the connection
will not work.
Conventionally, the calling device uses originating tones while the answering device uses answering tones. This
is not required, however, and crucially the 835 does not attempt to enforce this. This means that attempting to
answer a call without sending the J command to switch to answering tones will fail, as the modem will attempt to
use originating tones. Similarly, the I command must be used to switch back to originating tones before dialing
after answering a call.
$4B (K) – Pulse dial
The K command switches the 835 to pulse dialing mode, where it momentarily pulses the phone connection on-
hook to dial a number. Timing is automatically handled by the 835 such that the computer need only supply the
digits; the firmware automatically controls the pulse and interdigit timing and tells the computer when each new
digit can be supplied.
The controller issues a proceed pulse to the computer to indicate when it is ready for a digit, including before the
first digit and after each received digit is dialed. Each digit is sent from the computer as command byte from $x1-
$xA to indicate 1-10 pulses, corresponding to dialing 1-9 or 0. The upper nibble is masked off and ignored,
except for a Q byte which will reset the modem. Any byte with a lower nibble of $C-$F or $0 is ignored entirely
and will just result in the controller pulsing proceed to request another byte. (Note that this means that an
ATASCII ‘0’ will not work.) A lower nibble of $B ends pulse dialing and executes the off-hook (“L”) command,
which will also pulse the SIO proceed line upon completion.
The pulse dial command implicitly enables phone audio at the start of the dialing process.
$4C (L) – Pick up phone
The L command takes the phone off-hook, picking up the phone. This also begins the carrier detection process,
where the controller will wait up to 30 seconds to detect a carrier. SIO proceed is pulsed immediately after the
command is processed, without waiting for the carrier, and SIO interrupt is pulsed when the carrier is detected
(or subsequently lost).
The modem processing loop resumes execution during the 30 second wait for carrier and the modem can
process commands, particularly the M (hang up phone) command. If 30 seconds pass without a carrier being
detected, the modem will automatically hang up.
Unlike the pulse dial command, the pick up command does not enable phone audio.
$4D (M) – Hang up phone
The M command puts the phone back on-hook, hanging up. The controller waits for any previously received data
to finish sending, then hangs up and waits for carrier detect to drop. SIO proceed is not pulsed until this process
is complete.
Chapter 9 -  Serial I/O (SIO) Bus
255

--- Page 256 ---

Altirra Hardware Reference Manual
Created by Avery Lee
$51 (Q) – Reset modem
This command resets the modem, hanging up the phone, restoring it to default state. It is similar to power-on
initialization except for also pulsing proceed to tell the computer when reinitialization is complete.
The Q command is also notable for being accepted in many contexts where other commands are not. This
includes suspended mode and pulse dialing.
$52/$53 (R/S) – Enable/disable sound
The R and S commands enable and disable sound from the phone line being played through the TV speaker.
Sound is also automatically enabled at the start of dialing, and automatically disabled on modem reset, when a
carrier is detected or when hanging up, either manually or due to lost carrier. It is not automatically enabled when
manually picking up.
There is no support in the 835 for the opposite direction, playing computer sound on the phone line. This means
that the 835 cannot tone dial.
$57/$58 (W/X) – Set/clear analog loopback test
The W and X commands enable and disable analog loopback, respectively, where the analog output of the
modem is looped back to the input. This allows most of the modem short of the phone line to be tested without a
connection, with any byte sent being received back. The phone does not need to be taken off-hook to enable
analog loopback, and no pick up or hang up occurs when toggling it.
A side effect of enabling analog loopback is that the modem detects a carrier while it is enabled, because it
switches to using the same tones for both transmitting and receiving and the carrier detect logic senses the
modem’s own output.
$59 (Y) – Resume modem
Re-enables modem processing after suspension with the Z (suspend modem) command.
$5A (Z) – Suspend modem
Used to temporarily disable the modem so that the SIO bus can be used to connect to other devices.
Modem processing is resumed through the Y (resume modem) command.

## Known firmware

There is only one currently known version of firmware. The 1K internal ROM in the 8048 has a CRC32 of
D6DD4F41.
## Modem hardware

Bell 103 compatible modulation and demodulation is performed by a TMS99532 single-chip Bell 103 compatible
modem. It is a “dumb” modem that has no AT command processing and communicates with the MCU using
simple digital signals for serial data and control/sensing. Serial transmission over the modem is similar to the
SIO bus, with a low start bit, eight data bits sent int LSB to MSB order, and a high stop bit.
The 835 also has the ability to conduct audio from the phone line to SIO Audio In so it can be heard through the
TV speaker. It is enabled when bit 4 of P2 is pulled low.59 There is no support for conducting audio in the other
direction, from the computer to the phone line.
## 9.13 1030 Modem

The 1030 modem is an SIO bus peripheral that allows phone line based communications at 300 baud with Bell
103 modem compatible modulation. It is an improved version of the 835 with tone dialing and bootstrap support.

SIO command processing
The 1030 has two command modes, active and suspended. In suspended mode, SIO commands are
processed, while modem processing occurs in active mode. It powers up in and resets to suspended mode
whenever the computer is power-cycled, and transitions between the modes in response to commands.
In suspended mode, no modem carrier detection or data reception/transmission occurs as the controller is
occupied waiting for and processing SIO commands. Four commands are handled by the firmware:
Device $31 command $53 – disk status
- 
Device $31 command $52 – disk read sector
- 
Device $58 command $3B – download ModemLink
- 
Device $58 command $3C – download T: handler
- 
The firmware simultaneously monitors for standard SIO command frames at 19200 baud and 1030 command
bytes at 300 baud. If it receives a command byte at 300 baud of $51 (“Q”) or $59 (“Y”), it will execute the
corresponding Reset or Resume Modem command, and in the latter case, transition from SIO command
processing to modem processing. The command byte must be the first byte sent after SIO command is asserted
so the firmware can switch receive paths after detecting the framing error.
Fake disk boot
The computer can boot ModemLink firmware directly off of the 1030 by means of a fake disk boot, where the
1030 emulates a D1: disk drive. The fake disk drive will not activate until the 20th status command sent to D1:,
upon which the 1030 will respond with a plain $00 00 E0 00 status frame and then enable processing of its Read
Sector command to return a single boot sector. The boot sector checks if the T: handler is present and exits
silently if so (C=0); otherwise, it downloads and runs the ModemLink software.
The disk emulation does not respond to any other commands and will not even NAK them. Any valid but
unhandled command to D1:, including a Read Sector other than for sector 1, will not be responded to but will
reset the polling counter back to 20, disabling the Read Sector command.
Download commands
The boot sector returned by the 1030 uses SIO address $58, command $3B to download the ModemLink
software. This command returns a large $2800 byte data frame to be downloaded to $0C00-33FF, with a call to
$1D0C to initialize the T: handler and ModemLink being installed into DOSVEC with a start address of $0C00.
AUX1/AUX2 in the command frame are ignored. This command requires a device timeout of just over 6 seconds
to complete due to the long payload.
The T: handler embedded within the on-board ModemLink software can also be downloaded by itself using
address $58, command $3C. This returns $B30 bytes corresponding to the subset $1D00-282F within the full
ModemLink download. The initialization routine is at $1D0C. The T: handler is not relocatable.
Unlike the 850, there are no one-time restrictions on the download commands and the 1030 will respond to them
any number of times without requiring a reset process. However, the 1030 must be processing SIO commands
for this, and will not be able to respond if it is in modem processing mode.
Receive tones during download
While sending the ModemLink or T: handler software, different tones can be heard from the computer during the
transmission. This is caused by the 1030 sending data blocks from different areas of the firmware at slightly
different speeds. The baud rate is the same – 19200.0 baud – but the inter-byte delay varies.

Modem processing
When the modem is active, the modem processing loop takes over. SIO commands are not processed and are
ignored while this loop is active, but modem monitoring, communication, and 1030 command processing take
place simultaneously.
The 1030 continuously runs four shift registers in software: SIO input, SIO output, modem input, and modem
output. Shift processing occurs at 1200Hz with all four shifters running at 300 baud, so the 1030 can sample with
quarter bit phase precision. The firmware receives and retransmits bytes between the SIO and modem ports, so
bits are “reconditioned” in the process and are retimed at 300 baud regardless of the original transmission rate.
This also allows for one byte of buffering in each shift register, though the 1030 has no ability to catch up since
all shifters run at 300 baud and there is no provision for flow control.
The modem processing loop also monitors the SIO ready and carrier detect states. If SIO ready drops, indicating
that the computer is turned off, the 1030 will automatically reset itself and switch to SIO command processing.
Changes in carrier detect state are monitored to handle the various dial / answer processes.
Data protocol
When the modem connection is active, the computer and the 1030 modem exchange data directly on the bus at
300 baud, without using command or data frames. This means that the SIO bus is exclusively dedicated to the
modem during an online connection unless suspended using the $5A (“Z”) command. The 1030 does not use the
motor control line as the tape drives do.
Command protocol
Unlike other SIO peripherals, the 1030 uses a non-standard protocol for modem commands on the SIO bus. All
commands are sent as single characters at 300 baud with the command line asserted. There is no mechanism
to prevent other devices from receiving these bytes; they are simply expected to ignore them as invalid
command frames due to framing errors or invalid command frame checksums.

Commands $4E (“N”) and $52-56 (“R” through “V”) are ignored and not handled by the firmware. Some of them
are commands only supported by the 835 or XM301, or have different definitions in the T: handler software.
Compared to the 835, the 1030 adds the tone dialing and 30 second timeout commands, and removes the
enable/disable sound commands.
If the modem is suspended and thus processing SIO commands, only the Reset Modem (“Q”) and Resume
Modem (“Y”) commands are handled. All other commands are ignored.
The SIO command line should be asserted before the start of the byte and deasserted after the end of the byte.
The two processing modes have different quirks in this regard. The modem processing loop simply requires SIO
command to be asserted when the stop bit is processed. The SIO command processing loop requires the 300
baud command byte to be the first byte issued after the SIO command line is asserted.
Command validation bug
Command bytes in the range of $80-FF are ignored by the firmware, but bytes within $00-7F and outside of the
range $48-5A (H-Z) can cause the 1030 to malfunction. This is due to missing validation in the firmware,
resulting in it overrunning the bounds of a jump table and jumping to random locations within the code page that
handles commands. For example, the command byte $5F will lock up the 1030 firmware’s main thread and
prevent it from processing commands. This only applies when normal command processing is enabled and not
specialized command processing like dial loops or the SIO command loop monitoring for Q/Y commands.
Signaling
The 1030 modem is one of the rare devices that uses the SIO proceed and interrupt control lines. The proceed
line is used to signal that communication can proceed after a command, while the interrupt line indicates the
carrier detect state. These are intended to drive the PIA interrupt facility in order to assert IRQs on the 6502.
Both signals are momentarily pulled low for one tick at the modem processing rate of 1200Hz, lasting for 833μs.
The SIO proceed signal pulses when a command finishes or when a new byte is needed during a dial command,
and the SIO interrupt signal pulses on a change in the carrier detect state.
There is no dedicated reporting for changes in the on/off hook state. The handler software must infer the phone
being taken off-hook when dial commands are issued. The 1030 does indicate via the SIO proceed line when a
hang-up occurs due to carrier detect timeout.

Transitioning back to SIO command processing
Once in modem processing state, the 1030 does not monitor or process any SIO commands until it transitions
back to the SIO command processing. This happens in one of three cases:
The Suspend Modem (“Z”) command is issued.
- 
The Reset Modem (“Q”) command is issued.
- 
The computer is turned off (SIO ready deasserts).
- 
Notably, hanging up the modem does not end modem processing. This can pose problems when soft-resetting
the computer, as the 1030 will remain in the modem processing loop and fail to respond to disk boot or download
commands.
The typical solution is to power-cycle the computer so the 1030 can reset itself when the SIO ready signal drops.
However, software that specifically tries to download the T: handler from the 1030 can also send a Reset Modem
(“Q”) command at 300 baud with SIO command asserted to re-enable SIO command processing.
Command behavior
$48 (H) – Send break signal
Sends a long space (0 bit) signal to the remote side, often interpreted as a request to interrupt an operation. The
controller waits for any currently buffered bytes to finish shifting, then suspends the shifters and pulls the modem
transmit line low. After half a second, the transmit line is raised, the shifters are re-enabled, and regular
communication resumes. SIO proceed is pulsed both after the command and when the break is finished.
As the SIO input shifter is also suspended during this process, no commands can be issued until the break
completes.
$49/$4A (I/J) – Set originate/answer mode
These commands select the tone set used by the modem, choosing the “polarity” of the communication. One
side must use the originating tone pair while the other side must use the answering tone pair, or the connection
will not work.
Conventionally, the calling device uses originating tones while the answering device uses answering tones. This
is not required, however, and crucially the 1030 does not attempt to enforce this. This means that attempting to
answer a call without sending the J command to switch to answering tones will fail, as the modem will attempt to
use originating tones. Similarly, the I command must be used to switch back to originating tones before dialing
after answering a call.
$4B (K) – Pulse dial
The K command switches the 1030 to pulse dialing mode, where it momentarily pulses the phone connection
on-hook to dial a number. Timing is automatically handled by the 1030 such that the computer need only supply
the digits; the firmware automatically controls the pulse and interdigit timing and tells the computer when each
new digit can be supplied.
The controller issues a proceed pulse to the computer to indicate when it is ready for a digit, including before the
first digit and after each received digit is dialed. Each digit is sent from the computer as command byte from $x1-
$xA to indicate 1-10 pulses, corresponding to dialing 1-9 or 0. The upper nibble is masked off and ignored,
except for a Q byte which will reset the modem. Any byte with a lower nibble of $C-$F or $0 is ignored entirely
and will just result in the controller pulsing proceed to request another byte. (Note that this means that an
Chapter 9 -  Serial I/O (SIO) Bus
261

--- Page 262 ---

Altirra Hardware Reference Manual
Created by Avery Lee
ATASCII ‘0’ will not work.) A lower nibble of $B ends pulse dialing and executes the off-hook (“L”) command,
which will also pulse the SIO proceed line upon completion.
Pulses are issued by the firmware at a rate of 10 pulses/second with a make/break ratio of about 30%/70%. The
time for the controller to signal completion, the computer to send the next byte, and for the controller to start the
next digit results in an interdigit delay of about 630ms from the end of the last pulse from the last digit to the first
pulse of the next, or 730ms from pulse end to pulse end.
The 1030 does not have a speaker or connection for phone audio, and so the dial tone and dialing sounds are
not audible. A small chirp is audible from the 1030 itself from an internal relay whenever the phone is placed
back on-hook during pulse dialing or when hanging up.
$4C (L) – Pick up phone
The L command takes the phone off-hook, picking up the phone. This also begins the carrier detection process,
where the controller will wait up to 30 seconds to detect a carrier. SIO proceed is pulsed immediately after the
command is processed, without waiting for the carrier, and SIO interrupt is pulsed when the carrier is detected.
SIO proceed is not pulsed when the carrier is detected.
The modem processing loop resumes execution during the 30 second wait for carrier and the modem can
process commands, particularly the M (hang up phone) command. If 30 seconds pass without a carrier being
detected, the modem will automatically hang up and proceed is pulsed to indicate the hang up.
$4D (M) – Hang up phone
The M command puts the phone back on-hook, hanging up. The controller waits for any previously received data
to finish sending, then hangs up and waits for carrier detect to drop. SIO proceed is not pulsed until this process
is complete.
The controller does not return to SIO command processing mode when this command is issued – it remains in
modem processing mode. The Q (reset modem) command is needed to re-enable SIO commands on the
modem.
$4F (O) – Tone dial
Tone dialing is performed with the O command. Unlike pulse dialing where the controller does most of the work,
the 1030 only conducts the computer’s audio onto the phone line and the computer must generate the DTMF
tones. The standard T: handler does this through 4-bit volume only mode. Unlike pulse dialing, tone dialing is
audible as there is no way for the handler to play DTMF tones for the 1030 without also playing them through the
regular audio output.
Upon receiving the O command, the controller takes the phone off-hook, waits two seconds, then enables audio
pass-through and pulses proceed so the computer can play the DTMF tones. Afterward, the computer then
sends a Q command to reset the modem or a P command to end dialing and begin waiting for carrier, with any
other command byte or any non-command byte ignored. Either way, the audio pass-through is disabled and tone
dialing ends. Proceed is pulsed again after the P/Q command.
An oddity of this setup is that the SIO bus does not actually have an audio output; instead, the 1030 amplifies
leakage in the SIO audio in line to detect POKEY’s output. This can be unreliable depending on the computer
model or presence of other devices on the SIO bus, and the 1030’s documentation says that it does not work
with the 400.
$50 (P) – Start 30 second timeout
The P command disables the audio pass-through from tone dialing and takes the phone off-hook to wait for the
Chapter 9 -  Serial I/O (SIO) Bus
262

--- Page 263 ---

Altirra Hardware Reference Manual
Created by Avery Lee
carrier, using the same logic as the pick up phone (“L”) command. The only effective difference between the P
and L commands is that only P is accepted to end tone dialing; otherwise there is no difference as the audio
pass-through is already disabled when not tone dialing.
$51 (Q) – Reset modem
This command resets the modem, hanging up the phone, restoring it to default state, and re-enabling SIO
command processing. It is similar to power-on initialization except for also pulsing proceed to tell the computer
when reinitialization is complete.
The Q command is also notable for being accepted in many contexts where other commands are not. This
includes SIO command or suspended mode and pulse/tone dialing.
$57/$58 (W/X) – Set/clear analog loopback test
The W and X commands enable and disable analog loopback, respectively, where the analog output of the
modem is looped back to the input. This allows most of the modem short of the phone line to be tested without a
connection, with any byte sent being received back. The phone does not need to be taken off-hook to enable
analog loopback, and no pick up or hang up occurs when toggling it.
A side effect of enabling analog loopback is that the modem detects a carrier while it is enabled, because it
switches to using the same tones for both transmitting and receiving and the carrier detect logic senses the
modem’s own output.
$59 (Y) – Resume modem
Re-enables modem processing after suspension with the Z (suspend modem) command. The controller re-
enters the modem processing loop and pulses SIO proceed.
This command can also be used to begin modem processing after the modem powers up or is reset, since the
suspended flag is set whenever the modem is processing SIO commands.
$5A (Z) – Suspend modem
Used to temporarily disable the modem so that the SIO bus can be used to connect to other devices. The
controller waits for any currently shifting data to finish, then disables the shifters and pulses SIO proceed, after
which it switches to SIO processing mode. If a connection has been established, the phone stays off-hook and
the carrier is preserved, but no new data is sent and any received data is lost.
Modem processing is resumed through the Y (resume modem) command.
Carrier detection is also suspended, so the modem will not report loss of carrier over the SIO interrupt line.
However, it will reconcile and report a change once modem processing is resumed.
## 9.14 1030 Hardware

Controller
The 1030’s controller is an 8050 microcontroller running at a clock rate of 4.032MHz. This is a variant of the
8048 with 4K of internal ROM and 256 bytes of internal RAM. An additional 8K of external ROM is connected to
the MCU, but unlike the XF551, it is not used for program storage – it is used for extra data storage.
A substantial portion of the firmware is used to store the downloadable ModemLink and T: handler software for
the computer: the entirety of the 8K external ROM and about 60% of the internal 4K ROM.

## Known firmware

There is only one currently known version of firmware. The 4K internal ROM in the 8050 has a CRC32 of
329B1D5B, while the 8K external ROM has a CRC32 of 7ABDB8E7.
The internal firmware is highly similar to the 835 firmware for common features. The main differences are
## patches for the different hardware connections, added tone dialing support, removal of enable/disable sound

support, and SIO command processing.
## Modem hardware

Bell 103 compatible modulation and demodulation is performed by a TMS99532 single-chip Bell 103 compatible
modem. It is a “dumb” modem that has no AT command processing and communicates with the MCU using
simple digital signals for serial data and control/sensing. Serial transmission over the modem is similar to the
SIO bus, with a low start bit, eight data bits sent int LSB to MSB order, and a high stop bit.
POKEY audio output leaked through the SIO audio in line is amplified and connected to the TMS99532’s
external audio input (EXI). It is always connected, but the TMS99532 only passes it through to the analog output
when the transmitter squelch and the answer tone enable (/ATE) signals are asserted. This disables the normal
transmission and conducts only the external audio input. The 1030 does not have the ability to pass audio in the
other direction, from the phone line to the computer (the 835 and XM301 do).

## 9.15 SX212 Modem

The SX212 modem is a Hayes-compatible 1200 baud modem with both SIO and RS-232 connections. Like the
XM301 and unlike the 1030, it has no on-board software and a T: handler or communications program must be
loaded externally.
Command set
The SX212's command interface is handled by a Sierra Semiconductor SC11008 Stand-Alone Modem Interface
Controller. The following commands are supported:

| --- | --- |
| ATA | Answer (go off hook) |
| ATB | Set Bell modulation mode* |
| ATC | Set transmit carrier |
| ATD | Dial |
| ATE | Set echo |
| ATF | Set full duplex |
| ATH | Set on/off hook |
| ATI | Information |
| ATL | Speaker loudness* |
| ATM | Speaker mode |
| ATO | Originate (go off hook) |
| ATP | Set pulse dial mode |
| ATQ | Set quiet mode |
| ATR | Set reverse mode |
| ATS | Set or query register |
| ATT | Set touch dialing |
| ATV | Set verbose reporting |
| ATX | Set connect/busy/dialtone reporting |
| ATY | Set long space disconnect enable* |
| ATZ | Reset modem |

Commands marked with an asterisk (*) are ones that are documented in the SC11008 datasheet and supported
by the SX212, but not documented in the Atari SX212 Modem Owner's Manual.
Escape guard
Like truly Hayes-compatible modems, the SX212 requires appropriate guard time before and after the +++
escape sequence to recognize it as such. This is set in register S12 in 1/50th second units and defaults to one
Chapter 9 -  Serial I/O (SIO) Bus
265

--- Page 266 ---

Altirra Hardware Reference Manual
Created by Avery Lee
second. Attempting to use the time-independent escape sequence (TIES) used by some modems without
appropriate delays does not work.61
Version information
The ATI0 and ATI1 commands emit decimal numbers for the product code and firmware checksum of the
modem, respectively. On at least one modem, these values are 134 and 103.
SIO motor control line
Since the standard SIO command frame protocol is not used by the SX212, the motor control line is used
instead to indicate when communication with the modem is desired. Data is only received by and sent from the
SX212 when the motor control line is asserted low.
Conflicts on the motor control line are avoided because the SX212, like the 410 and 1010 Program Recorders,
only have one SIO connector and are designed to only be used at the end of the SIO chain.
SIO proceed/interrupt lines
The SX212 indicates the carrier detect and high speed states to the computer through the SIO proceed and
interrupt signals, respectively. These match the indicator lights such that the proceed line is low whenever CD is
on and the interrupt line is low when HS is on. Changes in these signals are then exposed to software via
connections to the CA1 and CB1 inputs on the PIA.
Because the PIA only allows edge detection on the CA1/CB1 inputs, an initialization sequence is necessary for
the handler software to ascertain the current state of the SIO proceed and interrupt lines before it can begin
tracking changes in the CD/HS states.
Speed auto-switching
Commands can be sent to the modem at either 300 or 1200 baud. When the character is received in command
mode, the modem will automatically switch to the correct speed. This flips both the state of the high speed (HS)
indicator and the SIO interrupt line. The character that triggers this switch is still recognized and processed
correctly.
The SX212 powers up in high-speed mode.
## 9.16 R-Verter

The R-Verter is a small adapter cable that connects an RS-232 serial device to the SIO bus.
Motor control line
The standard SIO protocol is not used by the R-Verter; the motor control line is used instead to enable
communications. When the motor control line is asserted (motor on), full-duplex transmit/receive and DTR
sensing are enabled; when it is negated, the R-Verter disconnects from the bus.
Communication parameters
The R-Verter does not have a UART or UART-like controller and simply adapts the SIO bus to an RS-232
[61] Not only does Atari's manual not document this either, the Atari SX212 modem handler tries to emit +++AT as part of its initialization
sequence without delays, even though the hardware is configured by default to require guard times.
Chapter 9 -  Serial I/O (SIO) Bus
266

--- Page 267 ---

Altirra Hardware Reference Manual
Created by Avery Lee
connector. This means that serial framing and timing are determined by POKEY, while parity and stop bit settings
are driven by software.
Carrier Detect and Data Set Ready sensing
The Carrier Detect (CD) and Data Set Ready (DSR) pins of the RS-232 connector are hooked up to the Proceed
and Interrupt lines on the SIO bus, respectively, with inversion. This means that an active CD/DSR line pulls
CA1/CB1 low.
## 9.17 410/1010 Program Recorder

The 410 and 1010 Program Recorders are cassette tape recorders with a connection to the SIO bus.
Motor control
The SIO motor control line enables the 410/1010 recorder motor under computer control, allowing the tape to be
stopped on demand. The Play or Record button must also be depressed on the 410 for the motor to activate.
The motor control line also serves as the voltage source for the audio track, cutting out the audio when the motor
is deactivated. A side effect of this is that rapid toggling of the motor control line will be reflected as audio on the
computer when the 410/1010 is connected.
Data decoding and encoding
During playback, the data track is processed by two bandpass filters centered at ~4kHz and ~5KHz. The
amplitudes of the two filters are compared and the result is sent across the SIO bus, with the 4KHz filter
producing a 0 and the 5KHz filter producing a 1. This decodes the frequency shift keying (FSK) encoding used to
record data onto the tape.
When recording, the SIO bus data is recorded directly onto the tape. This is normally done with two-tone mode
with timers 1 and 2 clocked with the 64KHz clock with divisors of 6 and 8 (AUDF1=5 and AUDF2=7), giving
5327Hz and 3995Hz as the two tones.
Serial data is recorded onto the tape LSB-first, so every byte is written with a start bit, bits 0 to 7, and then a stop
bit.
Turbo modifications
A popular modification to Atari cassette tape recorders involves adding a turbo mode that bypasses the FSK
bandpass filters. This allows for higher data rates to be recorded onto the tape, at the cost of additional
complexity to manually modulate the signal. This is often activated by lowering the command line.
## 9.18 MidiMate

The MidiMate provides MIDI capability over the SIO bus.
MIDI communications
MIDI messages are sent at 31250 baud, which is not a rate that POKEY can hit normally with sufficient accuracy.
Therefore, the MidiMate provides an external clock for POKEY to use, by dividing down a 4MHz crystal by 128.
This is then selected by software using the external input/output clocking modes in the SKCTL register. Software
is responsible for following the MIDI protocol for sent messages.
Chapter 9 -  Serial I/O (SIO) Bus
267

--- Page 268 ---

Altirra Hardware Reference Manual
Created by Avery Lee
Sync input
An external source can be connected to the MidiMate for timing synchronization purposes. This is connected to
the SIO bus interrupt line, which in turn connects to the CB1 input on the PIA.
Enable/disable
The SIO motor control line is used to enable the MidiMate. When asserted, the external serial clock and sync
input are enabled; otherwise, they are disconnected from the SIO bus.
## 9.19 Pocket Modem

The Pocket Modem, by BOT Engineering, is a small SIO-based, 300 baud modem.
Data transfers
POKEY's standard serial port functionality is used for full-duplex communication with the modem. There is no
setting for baud rate on the modem itself; the baud rate is determined solely by the rate at which POKEY sends
and receives data. Supported baud rates are 110, 210, 300, and 500 baud.
Command protocol
The Pocket Modem does not use the standard SIO command protocol. Instead, it uses a custom command
protocol based on both the command and motor control lines. The command line serves as the data line and the
motor line serves as a clock.
Each command provides the setting for four mode bits on the device. The bits, in shifting order are:
Bit 0: Enables data communication. When this is set, the modem transfers data between the SIO bus
- 
and the phone line.
Bit 1: Off-hook state. Takes the phone off-hook (1) to answer or dial, or places it on-hook (0) to hang up.
- 
Bit 2: Sets the carrier frequencies to originate (0) or answer (1).
- 
Bit 3: Enables dialing if set to 1.
- 
The command line is set to low for a 0 or high for a 1, and is shifted into the device on the falling edge (asserting
edge) of the motor control line. There does not appear to be a direct indicator of when the last bit is shifted. The
shift rate is very slow, about one bit every six video frames in the standard driver.
Commonly used modes include %0000 to hang up, %0011 for communication when originating a call, %0111 for
comm when answering a call, %0010 or %0110 when temporarily suspending a call for disk access, and %1010
when dialing.
Pulse dialing
Tone dialing is not supported by the Pocket Modem, but it does support pulse dialing. Pulse dialing is enabled by
switching to mode %1010, which takes the phone off hook and enables dialing mode. In dialing mode, the
command line is used to control the on-hook state, such that asserting command (low) takes the phone off-hook,
and negating command (high) places it back on-hook. Pulse dialing is then performed by pulsing the on-hook
state with timing under software control.

Altirra Hardware Reference Manual
Created by Avery Lee
Carrier detect
The SIO proceed line is used to communicate carrier detect state to the computer. It is asserted (low) when a
remote carrier is absent and negated (high) when a carrier is present.
Ring detect
Auto-answer is also supported by means of a ring detection signal on the SIO interrupt line. The Pocket Modem
sends pulses on the interrupt line whenever ringing is detected. It cannot answer the phone automatically, but
software can count the ring pulses and switch the Pocket Modem to on-hook answer mode once enough pulses
have arrived.
